newsitem.title: UK: Pharmacia gets US approval for AIDS drug.
newsitem.headline: Pharmacia gets US approval for AIDS drug.

text.p: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Monday approved a new AIDS drug made by Swedish-U.S. drugs group Pharmacia & Upjohn Inc under the agency's accelerated programme for drugs that fight HIV.
Rescriptor, or delavirdine, is a member of a new class of anti-HIV drugs knowns as non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs).

They affect the virus at a slightly different stage in its cycle from the existing drugs -- the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors such as Glaxo-Wellcome's AZT (Retrovir), and the protease inhibitors.
NNRTIs have been enthusiastically greeted by AIDS researchers, who say they show strong effects in multi-drug cocktails.

Researchers at Montreal's McGill University studied the effects of AZT and Bristol Myers Squibb's ddI combined with Boehringer Ingelheim's Boehringer Mannheim Gmbh NNRTI nevirapine (Viramune) and found the triple drug cocktail knocked the virus back to undetectable levels in 75 percent of patients.
Pharmacia said Rescriptor also worked well.

"Patients treated with a combination of Rescriptor plus AZT showed a significantly greater reduction in the amount of virus in the blood for one year when compared with patients treated with AZT alone," Pharmacia said in a statement released in London.
But use of the drug did not affect survival or the appearance of AIDS-defining illnesses such as Kaposi's sarcoma, a common cancer among victims.

Unlike Viramune, Rescriptor seemed to enhance the effects of protease inhibitors. When used in combination with Merck's Crixivan (indinavir), it increased the blood level of indinavir, Pharmacia said.
Donald Batts, director of infectious diseases for Pharmacia, said this could be a benefit because protease inhibitors were expensive and had to be taken several times a day.
"There is the potential to convert some of the protease inhibitors to twice a day dosing which would dramatically increase compliance," he said in a telephone interview.
But protease inhibitors like Roche's saquinavir (Invirase) could increase levels of liver enzymes -- a concern to AIDS patients already at risk of hepatitis.
Both Viramune and Rescriptor can also cause skin rashes, but Batts said the effect went away after a few weeks. He said the cause was not clear.

Experts say NNRTIs offer new choices to AIDS patients taking one or two drugs who suffer a resurgence of the virus. Once the virus mutates into a resistant form, doctors fear it will resist other drugs in the same class.
But having a new class of drugs to give the patients means they have not used up all their opportunities for treatment.

Pharmacia spokesman John Ruane said the company's next step would be to test triple- and quadruple combinations including Rescriptor in HIV-positive volunteers. "We have not done head-to-head trials with Viramune yet," he added.
